notesStmt.note: The manuscript is written on the inside of several envelopes, two of which are postmarked in 1883 (one in November and another in December), suggesting that the draft was composed between then and the pieces's publication in February 1884. The cancelled section of text near the top of the second leaf is written on a scrap that was originally pasted behind the scraps above and below it, as a means of joining them together. The scrap has since become detached, revealing that it contained an earlier draft of the text that was pasted on top of it. Since the backing scrap is now exposed, we have chosen to transcribe it and mark it as deleted text.

This maunscript contains a draft of an essay which was first published in Baldwin's Monthly in February 1884 as "Reminiscences of the Indian Bureau." It was later included in November Boughs (1888) under the title "An Indian Bureau Reminiscence."

body.head: An Indian Bureau Reminiscence
body.p:
At After the close of the Secession war in '65 I worked for several months, (until Mr. Harlan turned me out for writing "Leaves of Grass,") in the Interior Department at Washington, in the Indian Bureau. Along this time ‸there came to Washington to see their Great Father, an unusual number of Indian aboriginal visitors, delegations for treaties, settlement of lands, ‸&c.,—
groups of chiefs —some young and middle aged, and some but mainly old men, from the West, North, and occasionally from the South—‸—several hundreds of them, in parties of from five twenty each the most wonderful specimens proofs of what Nature can produce,
(the survival of the fittest, no doubt, and the all the frailer samples, ‸dropt, sorted out,
by death)—‸—as if to show how the earth and woods, the attrition of storms and elements and the exigencies of life at first hand can train and fashion men—, and what they can turn out— indeed chiefs, men

There were Omaha, Poncas, Winnebagoes, and many others. Let me give a running account of what I see and hear through one of these exhibitions at the Indian Bureau, going back to the present tense.
2 ¶ There are are Omahas, Poncas, Winnebagos, &c. Let me, ‸for one of these exhibitions at the Indian office, give a running account of what I see and hear going back to the present tense
Every physique and head h and face here is impressive; Nature redeems herself, out of her crudest recesses. Most have red paint on their cheeks, however—or some other paint. ("Little Hill" makes a ‸the opening speech, which the interpreter translates by scraps.) Many ‸wear head tires of gaudy colored braid, wound around thickly—some with circlets thick with of eagles' feathers. χ nNecklaces of bears' claws are plenty around their necks. Most of the n of the chiefs are wrapt in large blankers of the brighest scarlet. ‸Two or three have blue, and I see one black. (A wise man called "the Flesh" ‸now makes a short speech, apparently asking something. Indian Commissioner Dole is answering answers him, and the interpreter translates in scraps again.) All the ‸principal chiefs have tomahawks or hatchets, some of them very richly ornamented and costly. Plaid shirts are to be observed—none too clean. Now a tall fellow
"Hole-in-the⹀Day," is speaking. He has a copious head⹀dress ‸composed of feathers and narrow ribbon, under which appears a countenance painted all over a bilious yellow. Let us note this young chief., ‸however. For all his paint, "Hole-in-the-Day" is a handsome Indian, very gentlemanly, mild and calm, dressed in black drab buckskin leggings, and a drab dark gray surtout, ‸and a soft black hat. His costume is perfect ‸will bear full observation, and even fashion would accept him.
His apparel is worn loose and scant enough to show a his superb physique, especially in neck, chest and legs. (The
‸Apollo Belvidere!" was the involuntary exclamation of a famous European artist when he first saw a good specimen of a ‸full⹀grown young Choc Choctaw.)
